doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

title: The Monkees' Daydream Believer and surgical edits with Tom Scott
summary: Hank cannot recall the flugelhorn part on the Monkees song, then describes long tape-splice transitions and mix moves with Tom Scott.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: I’m going to test your memory here. Did you, when you worked with the Monkees did you record the tune “Daydream Believer?”
There’s a moment near the end of that song where this flugelhorn comes in with this beautiful countermelody [scats]. Do you remember that?
No. It’s amazing with those kind of things, I know I understand that but actually I did that six months ago. You know? I don’t remember what I did six months ago.
Yeah, I know. It’s just this — I’ve always loved that moment and I’m curious which studio cat played that.

I’ll tell you the things — I got into a thing a couple of times with Tom Scott but what we actually did was it was a transition from one tune to another tune where you could just do it with two pots. But there were a couple of times where Tom wanted to keep the thing going a little longer so you had the cut that you normally would make, this is not going to work. We would do these really surgical things. You’d take, instead of Editall block, which is really six inches, you take two pieces of masking tape and put them down and put the tape between them and you can make a long splice and you’ve got a six inch edit. You’ve made a transition if you could do it with two pots it’s one thing to another mix. But if you’re trying to tape that mix together I’ve done that many times, and you’re cross- fading between two pieces. You’d be better right when you’re cutting that kind of stuff.
Yeah he told me that you would do mixes where you had sixteen faders and he had sixteen and I can almost picture how that, “No, no, not yet, don’t push that up yet.”
It happens occasionally. But if you’re a good editor nobody’s ever going to bother you with that stuff.
